headline: Block Island bass bite fires as thermal break sets up on Southwest Ledge
subhead: 62-degree island water creates feeding zone while mainland bays hit 74 degrees.
body_markdown:
The thermal break is here, and it's everything we've been waiting for. Block Island water dropped to 62.4 degrees this week while the mainland bays are cooking at 74 — that 12-degree spread is what makes this place the summer bass Mecca of the East Coast. When you've got that kind of temperature differential, the fish have no choice but to stack up on our ledges.

The Southwest Ledge has been the star of the show. I'm seeing consistent bass in the 28- to 35-pound class working the 45- to 60-foot contour where that cold, oxygenated water meets the warmer shelf water. The key depth has been 52 feet — that's where the thermocline is setting up, and it's holding bait like a magnet. Live peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig is the ticket, but you need to get them down fast in this current. I'm running 6-ounce bank sinkers to punch through, then letting the bait work in that sweet spot just above the ledge.

The North Rip has been producing too, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing. The current screams through there, but when it slacks off, the bass move up from the deep water to feed. I pulled a 38-pounder Tuesday morning on a live eel, drifted right along the edge where the rip breaks. The trick is reading the water — when you see that foam line start to dissipate, that's your window.

Fluke fishing has been solid around the windmill area. The turbine foundations are holding bait, and the fluke are stacked up in 35 to 45 feet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are working, but you need to work them slow. The current around those structures can be tricky — I'm using a long drift to cover water, then circling back when I mark fish. Keepers have been running 20 to 24 inches, with a few doormat-class fish mixed in.

Sea bass are everywhere right now. The rocky bottom around the island is loaded with keeper-sized fish, and they're not picky about baits. Clam strips on high-low rigs are producing steady action in 30 to 50 feet. The wind farm structures are holding fish too, though the current can make it challenging to hold bottom. I'm seeing limits of sea bass mixed with keeper porgies on most trips.

The bait situation is what's driving this bite. Sand eels are thick around the ledges, and I'm seeing massive schools of peanut bunker moving through. The cooler water is concentrating everything — bait, bass, blues, the whole food chain. When water temperatures are this perfect, Block Island becomes a feeding station for fish from hundreds of miles away.

Weather has been the wild card. We've got 8-foot seas building from the southwest, which is keeping some boats at the dock. But for those willing to make the run, the fishing has been worth the bumpy ride. The key is timing your trips — early morning has been best before the wind builds.

Bluefish are mixed in with the bass, mostly in the 5- to 8-pound class. They're hitting the same baits, same depths, but they're not as concentrated. I'm seeing them more scattered along the 40-foot line, picking off bait that gets pushed up from the deeper water.

Looking ahead, this thermal pattern should hold through the weekend. The new moon is coming Sunday, which means spring tides and stronger currents. That should push even more bait around the ledges and fire up the bite. I'm watching for the wind to lay down — if we get a calm morning, the Southwest Ledge is going to be the place to be. The bass are here, the bait is here, and the water temperature is perfect. This is what we wait all year for at Block Island.
